1016.title: Theophany: blessing the waters
1016.hook: Orthodox priests throw a cross into rivers and sea, and swimmers dive for it
1016.howItsDone: On Theophany, Orthodox and other Eastern churches celebrate the Great Blessing of the Waters, in church and often outdoors at a river, lake or sea, where a cross may be thrown in and retrieved by swimmers; families take blessed water home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epiphany: chalk above the door, and the wise men coming into the house. Your line was bless this house.

A crowd packs the edge of a harbor on a January morning. Young men stand along the dock in swim shorts, shivering, eyes on a priest in gold vestments holding up a wooden cross. The priest throws the cross, spinning, out over the water. It lands with a splash, and the swimmers hit the water after it. One comes up holding it over his head, soaked and grinning, and the crowd cheers. It happens in Greek towns, in Orthodox parishes by rivers and lakes, and on seashores far from Greece.
screen: `THE CROSS SPINS OUT OVER THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Theophany means God appearing, God made visible. For Orthodox and other Eastern Christians, it's a great January feast, and it remembers one scene above all: the baptism of Jesus in the river Jordan. Matthew tells it: "And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Look at who is there. The Son in the river, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice from heaven. Eastern Christians see the Trinity shown in one moment, at a riverbank. Then the turn that explains the harbor. Orthodox Christians teach that Jesus didn't go into the Jordan to be made clean. He went in to make the water holy, so that all water, every river, every sea, could carry blessing. So on this day the priest blesses water, often outdoors, at a river, lake or sea. Families carry bottles of it home, drink a little, sprinkle their rooms, and keep some for the year. The cross thrown into the harbor acts it out: it goes down into the water, the way Christ went down into the Jordan, and comes back up. A psalm says: "The voice of the LORD is upon the waters." Western churches remember the baptism too, soon after Epiphany; the Eastern feast blesses the water itself.
screen: `NOT TO BE CLEANSED, BUT TO BLESS.`

segments.voice: Pour a glass of water and hold it in both hands: water you didn't make, that fell as rain somewhere and ran through rivers and pipes to reach you. If you pray, you can trace a cross over it, as some Orthodox families do with the water they bring home, and give thanks in the psalm's words, the voice of the Lord is upon the waters; if you don't, simply be thankful for it. Then drink it slowly.
Theophany. God made visible: the Eastern feast of Christ's baptism in the Jordan, when the waters are blessed and the cross is thrown into the sea.
Your line: the waters blessed. Every river, every sea. Until next time.

1017.title: Prayer for Christian unity (18–25 January)
1017.hook: a week when churches pray for each other
1017.howItsDone: During the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, churches of different traditions hold shared services, swap pulpits or choirs, and include one another by name in their prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Theophany: a cross thrown into cold water, and your line was the waters blessed.

On a weeknight in January, a Lutheran pastor reads a prayer out loud, and the name in it belongs to the Catholic parish two streets over. Across town, an Orthodox priest asks God's blessing on a Pentecostal church that meets in a former shop. A Methodist choir sings in a Baptist chapel, and nobody tries to sign anybody up. For one week, churches that disagree about baptism, bishops and bread pray for each other by name. Not to settle the arguments. Just to pray. Behind that week sits a single night, a table, and a prayer Jesus prays for people who will come after his friends.
screen: `A PRAYER WITH ANOTHER CHURCH'S NAME IN IT.`

segments.voice: John's Gospel slows right down on the night before Jesus dies. After the supper and the long talk, he looks up and prays, and all of chapter seventeen is that prayer. Partway through, he turns from the friends in the room to everyone who will come after them. In the King James Bible: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me." It isn't a rule; nobody is ordered to be one. It's a request, made to God. And notice the pattern: one the way the Father and the Son are one. Not identical, not merged into a single shape. Close, and turned toward each other. Churches don't use it to pretend their differences are gone. Catholics, Orthodox Christians and Protestants still hold different views about how the church is ordered, who presides at communion, and what unity would finally look like. Some hope for one visible church. Some think unity already exists underneath the different names. The week doesn't decide between them. It asks each church to pray the prayer Jesus prayed, and to say the other church's name while doing it. And the last clause: that the world may believe. How Christians treat each other is part of how anyone hears the message. A family that only argues is hard to listen to.

Bring to mind a church you've never set foot in: the unfamiliar name on the corner, a chapel you pass on the bus, a congregation that worships in a language you don't speak. Picture the door, the people going in, someone setting out chairs. If you pray, hold that church before God by name and ask good things for it; if you don't, simply wish it well, the people inside and the work they do.
Hen. Greek for one, the word in Jesus's prayer that the Father and the Son, and all who follow, may be one.
Your line: that they may be one. Asked for, not ordered. See you tomorrow.

1018.title: St Brigid (1 February)
1018.hook: Irish families weave rush crosses for the spring
1018.howItsDone: In Ireland, families and schools weave Brigid's crosses from rushes or straw around her feast day, often hanging the new cross by the door or in the kitchen and taking down last year's.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hen: churches praying for each other by name, and your line was that they may be one.

A bundle of green rushes lies on a kitchen table, still damp from the ditch. Someone folds one stalk over another, turns the bundle, folds again, and slowly a small square appears in the middle with four arms reaching out. Tie the ends with thread: a cross that looks a little like a pinwheel. In Ireland, families make these at the start of February and hang them over the door or in the kitchen, and last year's comes down. Not carved: woven from whatever grows by the field. Behind the custom is a woman, a sickbed, and a story about explaining the faith with what was lying on the floor.

Tradition honors Brigid of Kildare as one of Ireland's patron saints. What's told about her comes from lives of the saint written after her time; the Bible doesn't mention her. The stories show a woman who led a community at Kildare and gave things away, sometimes alarmingly: one has her handing her father's sword to a poor man so he could sell it for food. The cross comes from another story. Tradition says Brigid was called to the bedside of a dying chieftain who did not share her faith. He was restless and couldn't be calmed. The floor was strewn with rushes, the way floors were then, so she sat down, picked some up, and wove a cross while she talked about the man who died on one. The story says he grew quiet, listened, and asked to be baptized before he died. That's Brigid's faith in the stories: practical, made from whatever was at hand. Not gold, not marble. Rushes. Her day falls at the hinge of the Irish year, when the worst of winter is turning and the first lambs come. Some readers note that the turn of spring was marked in Ireland before Christianity too, and that Brigid's day gathered up that older season. So the cross over the door carries two hopes: her faith, and the light coming back. The Song of Solomon puts the second one this way: "For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; The flowers appear on the earth."
screen: `A WOMAN OF KILDARE, KNOWN BY TRADITION.`
`MADE FROM WHAT WAS ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Make a simple cross from whatever is near: two pencils and a rubber band, two twigs, two straws. It doesn't need to be beautiful; Brigid's came from the floor. As your hands work slowly, think of one thing you're waiting on to turn, the way winter turns, and if you pray, hold it before God as you finish.
St Brigid. A saint of Kildare, remembered in tradition for generous hands and a cross woven from rushes at a dying man's bed.
Your line: spring is coming. The light comes back. That's day one thousand eighteen.

1019.title: Candlemas (2 February)
1019.hook: forty days after Christmas: Simeon's light, and candles blessed
1019.carry: a light to lighten the gentiles
1019.howItsDone: At Candlemas, Catholic, Anglican and some Lutheran churches bless candles and carry them in procession; Orthodox churches keep the same feast as the Meeting of the Lord, and Simeon's song is sung at evening prayer in several traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Brigid and a cross woven from floor rushes, and your line was spring is coming.

Two small birds. That's the offering a young couple bring to the temple in Jerusalem, along with their baby. The law in Leviticus says that after the birth of a son the mother waits seven days, then thirty-three more, and then brings a lamb, or, if she can't afford one, two turtledoves or two young pigeons. Mary and Joseph come with the birds. In the crowded courts, one man has been waiting for something only he knows about. Churches keep this day in early February, counting from Christmas, and in some churches it begins with candles. Today's word is what the couple came to do.

Luke tells it in the King James Bible: "And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord." That's the Presentation: a firstborn son brought to the temple and offered back to God, as the law asks. Then Simeon. Luke says he was just and devout, and that the Holy Ghost had shown him he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ. So he has been waiting, scanning faces. When this couple with their two birds walks in, he knows. He takes the baby in his arms, blesses God, and says words some churches still sing at the close of the day: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation, Which thou hast prepared before the face of all people; A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel." Simeon is holding a baby who hasn't said a word, and he calls him light, for his own people and for everyone outside them. Light is at the heart of the day's English name, Candlemas. In some churches candles are blessed and carried in procession against the February dark, in some places the candles for the year ahead. Orthodox Christians call the feast the Meeting, because Simeon and the child meet. Catholics and Anglicans often call it the Presentation. Simeon's part ends with a man at peace, ready to go, because he got to hold the light.

Light a candle, or switch on one small lamp in a dim room, and look at it. Think of something you've waited a long time to see, and whether it came. If you pray, say Simeon's words slowly, Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace; if not, let your shoulders drop, like someone whose long wait is over.
Presentation. The baby brought to the temple and offered to God, where Simeon took him in his arms and called him a light.
Your line: a light to lighten the gentiles. Day one thousand nineteen, done.

1020.title: Shrove Tuesday
1020.hook: confess and use up the rich food before Lent: pancakes
1020.howItsDone: On the Tuesday before Ash Wednesday, families and churches in Britain, Ireland and elsewhere make pancakes, and some parishes hold pancake suppers or races; in other places the same day is kept as Mardi Gras or Carnival.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Candlemas: Simeon holding a baby and calling him light, and your line was a light to lighten the gentiles.

Eggs, butter, milk, a bag of flour, a bit of sugar. On one Tuesday a year, in kitchens across Britain, Ireland and plenty of other places, it all goes into one bowl and comes out as a stack of pancakes. Lemon and sugar for some, syrup for others, and a flip that lands on the floor at least once. In New Orleans the same day is Mardi Gras, French for fat Tuesday, with parades. It looks like a party, and it is. But the old English name for the day isn't about food. It's about the other thing people did before Lent: they went to church and told the truth about themselves. Today's word is shrove.

To shrive is an old English verb: to hear someone's confession and declare them forgiven. Shrove is its old past form, and shriven is what you are afterward: confessed, and let go. So Shrove Tuesday was the day you got shriven, cleared out before Lent began the next morning with Ash Wednesday. The letter of James puts it plainly, in the King James Bible: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." Notice the direction. One to another: not only up to God, but across, to a person. And the reason given isn't shame. It's healing. Churches practice this differently. Catholics and Orthodox Christians have the sacrament of confession with a priest. Anglicans offer it, and some use it. Some Protestant churches confess together, out loud, in a shared prayer, or between friends. Then the pancakes. Lent was traditionally a time of fasting from rich foods, and in some places that meant eggs, butter and milk. A kitchen full of them would spoil, or tempt. So you used them up, cooked everything rich in the house and fed everyone you could. Put the two halves together: empty the heart, then empty the pantry. Say what's wrong, then sit down and eat with the people who know. The feast comes after the truth is told.

Ask yourself, gently, what you'd want to set down before a fresh start: not a list, one thing, like a sharp word or a promise you let slide. Name it once, honestly, and if you pray, tell it to God plainly and ask to be let go of it. Then let your mind turn to the table, and to who you'd love to share a meal with.
Shrove. The old past form of shrive: to hear a confession and set someone free of it. The day before Lent, named for clearing out the heart.
Your line: shriven and fed. An old word with a stack of pancakes on top. Until tomorrow.

1021.title: Clean Monday
1021.hook: the Orthodox begin Lent on a Monday with kites, simple food, and forgiveness asked of everyone
1021.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians attend Forgiveness Vespers on the Sunday evening before Lent, where each person asks forgiveness of the others; on Clean Monday they begin the Lenten fast from meat and dairy, and in Greece families often picnic outdoors and fly kites.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shrove Tuesday: the heart cleared out, then the pantry, and your line was shriven and fed.

"Forgive me." The words go down a line of people in an Orthodox church on a Sunday evening. The priest bows to the first person in the congregation and asks it. Then that person turns to the next. Old women ask teenagers. Husbands ask wives. Someone asks the neighbor they haven't spoken to since the autumn. By the end, the line has reached everyone. The next morning, in Greece, families drive out to the hills with bread, olives and vegetables, no meat, no cheese, and fly kites against the sky. A day of forgiveness, then a day of wind and plain food. The Orthodox begin Lent on a Monday. Today, Clean Monday.

Yesterday was the Western way into Lent, with confession and pancakes before Ash Wednesday. Orthodox churches keep their own calendar for the season, and their Lent opens differently: on a Monday, and not with ashes but with a long chain of people asking pardon. The Sunday before is Forgiveness Sunday. Its Gospel includes Jesus's words from the Sermon on the Mount, in the King James Bible: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." So the church takes it literally. Before the fast starts, everyone asks forgiveness of everyone, whether or not they think they did anything wrong. It isn't a trial. Nobody has to prove who started it. The point is to go into the season with nothing owed. Then comes Monday, called clean in two ways. Clean in the kitchen: the meat and dairy are gone, and the food turns simple. And clean in the heart, which is why the forgiveness came first. The prophet Isaiah has a line that could hang over the whole day: "Wash you, make you clean." And the kites? Nobody in the Bible flies one. In Greece they're simply part of how families keep the day, outdoors, together, looking up. Some readers like the picture: a season that begins with eyes lifted and the weight a little lighter, on a hillside with the people you just asked to forgive you.

Bring to mind one person you'd ask to forgive you: a sibling, a coworker, a friend gone quiet. In the Orthodox custom you ask even when you're not sure what you did. Picture their face and say the two words to them in your mind, forgive me, and if you pray, bring them before God; if not, just hold them kindly.
Clean Monday. The first day of Lent in Orthodox churches, after a night of everyone asking forgiveness: clean food, clean heart, and kites in the air.
Your line: forgive me. Two words, and nothing owed. That's day one thousand twenty-one.

1022.title: Forty days
1022.hook: Moses on the mountain, Elijah on the road, Jesus in the desert
1022.howItsDone: During Lent, Christians often take on a practice for the season, such as fasting, giving something up, extra prayer, or giving to the poor, and churches connect the season to Jesus's forty days in the wilderness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clean Monday: a line of people asking pardon, and your line was forgive me.

A man alone on a mountain, with no bread and no water, while a cloud rests on the peak. Another, worn out and wanting to die, asleep under a juniper tree in the desert until someone wakes him and puts food beside his head. A third, just baptized, walking into the wilderness with nothing. Three stories from different parts of the Bible, and the same span of time turns up in all three. Not a week. Not a year. Long enough to hurt, and long enough to change you. Today, forty days.

Start with Moses. In Exodus he goes up to meet God and stays. The King James Bible says: "And he was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights; he did neither eat bread, nor drink water." He comes down carrying the words of the covenant on stone. Then Elijah. He has run for his life and lain down to die, and an angel brings him bread and water, twice. "And he arose, and did eat and drink, and went in the strength of that meat forty days and forty nights unto Horeb the mount of God." On that mountain he hears God not in the wind or the earthquake or the fire, but in a still small voice. And then Jesus. Matthew says: "And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred." The tempter comes, and Jesus answers him with words from scripture. Set the three side by side. Each is hard: hunger, exhaustion, testing. Each is spent close to God, away from the usual noise. And each one ends. Moses comes down. Elijah arrives. Jesus walks out to begin his work. The forty is not a life sentence; it's a passage with a far side. That's why churches link Lent to these stories, above all to Jesus in the desert: a season long enough for something to shift, and short enough to see the end of. This week ran from the waters of Theophany through prayer for unity, Brigid's rushes and Simeon's candle, to pancakes and a line of people saying forgive me. The last two stand at the very door of the forty days.

Let a few ideas come for one small thing you could keep for forty days: a walk each morning, a psalm a day, or giving up something that takes too much room. Pick one, not just the first, and picture day forty. If you pray, offer the forty days to God; if not, just hold the choice.
Forty days. The span of Moses on the mountain, Elijah on the road, and Jesus in the desert. A hard passage, close to God, that comes to an end.
Your line: forty is enough. Every forty has a far side. Rest well.

chat.says: Why is Lent forty days? Is it just a random number?
options: It echoes Moses, Elijah and Jesus: forty hard days close to God, that end.
It's the number of days Jesus spent in the tomb before Easter.
It's a round number for a long time, with no story behind it.
chat.meaning: Moses on the mountain, Elijah on the road and Jesus in the desert each spent forty days. Churches link Lent above all to Jesus's forty.

Elijah.meaning: a prophet of Israel who fled into the desert

Horeb.meaning: the mount of God, where Elijah heard a still small voice

covenant.meaning: God's binding promise with Israel, given through Moses

Lent.meaning: the season before Easter that churches link to these forties
